To an individual; but a congregation — whenever they repent and cry out with a whole heart — they are answered; as it is stated (Deuteronomy 4:7): "as Hashem our God is in all things that we call upon Him for."
column12: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 52:21–24
column13: And this is Deuteronomy 4:7: “For what great nation is there that has God so near unto them, as the Lord our God is in all things that we call upon Him” — showing that Israel possesses the distinction of having both Names combined, from which enduring vitality sustains the world, bounty ascending from this world to the world above from realm to realm, and subsequently descending from the highest world down to earth, as it is written (Isaiah 6:3): “And one called to another,” rendered: “and they receive one from another.”

column4: Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 9 — The Patriarchal Blessings and the Three Divine Attributes
column9: Genesis 26:3: ‘Reside in this land, and I will be with you and bless you; I will assign all these lands to you and to your heirs, fulfilling the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 9 — The Patriarchal Blessings and the Three Divine Attributes, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Genesis 26:3) to illuminate his statement here (“which hints at Yitzchak, unto whom it was explicitly commanded: 'Sojourn in this land' (Genesis 26:3); and the attribute of Yitzchak is contraction (Tzimtzum), for he saw that of all the converts of his father none...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: Whereas Abraham and Isaac during famines were compelled to migrate from their place, and we do not find miracles breaking nature performed for their sustenance, for their prospering and accumulating wealth occurred through Hashem's blessing channeled within the natural course of the world. Yet regarding Isaac it is stated: "and Hashem blessed him, and the man waxed great..." [Genesis 26:12–13], divine blessing being distinctly recognizable, for he fathered Jacob, wherefore "out of the north comes golden splendor" [Job 37:22], gold (Gevurah/North) not being food itself but the purchasing medium through which all human provisions are bought.
column12: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 34:9–12
column13: Forthwith Moses pleaded and would not let the Holy One go until he offered his life to death; whereas Noah did not do so, seeking personal deliverance while leaving the world; and whenever judgment is unleashed, the Holy Spirit laments: Woe that there is none found like Moses. For Moses had the Patriarchs upon whom to lean, crying out: “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants”; whereas Noah beheld preceding shattered worlds leaving only the cry “For You have lifted me up, and cast me down,” the mist of Ed (Adonai) ascending from the earth —.

column11: And this is the entire purpose of creating this physical world: that His glory, blessed be He, be revealed before the eyes of all, as written (Ta'anit 31a): in the future He will make a circle dance for the righteous, etc., and each one points to Him with a finger: "Behold, this is our God, etc."; and this is achieved through the deeds of the Torah and mitzvot in this world, as written in Shabbat (89b): that Isaac showed them the Holy One, blessed be He, with their own eyes; which derives from his spiritual level.

column9: Genesis 2:19: ‘And the ETERNAL God formed out of the earth all the wild beasts and all the birds of the sky, and brought them to the Human to see what he would call them; and whatever the Human called each living creature, that would be its name.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 9 — The Patriarchal Blessings and the Three Divine Attributes, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Genesis 2:19) to illuminate his statement here (“as written regarding Adam: 'and whatsoever the man called every living creature, that was its name' (Genesis 2:19); and 'I will make great' (agadlah) from Gedulah signifies expansion; meaning: 'and I will make your...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And so regarding Name and Remembrance: relative to the mortal recipient who recalls, he experiences a more tangible sensory grasp in remembering the subject than in his abstract name. Yet in reality the truth is the reverse: the Name is the core essence of vitality, as written: "whatever Adam called every living creature, that was its name" (Genesis 2:19).
column12: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 41:12–17
column13: Prior to the Flood, animals dwelled in pristine perfection, mating strictly after their kind, perceiving their root; wherefore Adam was forbidden to eat them, needing no human elevation, being whole in themselves. Adam was permitted only vegetation and fruit, which lacked the higher perfection of animal life; as seen in Adam naming beasts and birds, but not vegetation; naming them meaning binding them to their root to recognize their purpose; as in Zohar and Bahir: “and whatsoever the man called every living creature, that was the name thereof”—that was its essence.

column4: Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 9 — The Patriarchal Blessings and the Three Divine Attributes

Ka'avor), explained this: when the Blessed Name conducts His world in a garment termed “whirlwind” (sufah)—meaning through the concentrated intensity of a single attribute— the righteous aligned with that attribute surge in tremendous power that the generation finds hard to bear.

column11: And we begin to count the Omer immediately at night prior to the daytime bringing of the Omer offering; for immediately on the morrow of the Passover sacrifice begins the revelation of this counting, following the eating of the "bread of poverty" (lechem oni) of Pesach which catalyzes and introduces the bringing of this Omer. For in truth on the night of Pesach itself there exists countering the lechem oni which signifies contraction (tzimtzum), the eating of the meat of the Pesach offering which signifies expansiveness (harchavah).
